MEDI2004 · Week 4 · Pharmacodynamics (L7 + L8)

Pharmacodynamics — what drugs do, and how much

Pharmacokinetics was what the body does to the drug; pharmacodynamics is the reverse — what the drug does to the body, and how. This guide merges the two week-4 lectures: the targets drugs bind, the language of binding (specificity, selectivity, affinity), and how we quantify an effect with concentration–response curves — agonists, antagonists, efficacy and potency. Built from your lectures, using their own figures.

Covers L7 + L8 (4 learning objectives) Figures 9 plates from your lectures Recall 4 section checklists

§0Drug targets · L7

Where drugs act — the four targets

To understand what a drug does, first find what it binds.

Pharmacokinetics (PK) is the study of how the body handles drugs; pharmacodynamics (PD) is what the drug does to the body and how it does it — its mechanism of action. Since PD is the molecular story of a drug binding a target to produce a response, everything starts with the target. Most targets are proteins (a number that will grow with gene therapy), and a drug can activate, block/inhibit, or modulate them. There are four main protein targets — Plate 0.1 is the map for the whole lecture.

Label Key — the four targets (A–D)
A · Receptors
An agonist binds and triggers transduction (ion-channel opening, enzyme activation, DNA transcription); an antagonist occupies the receptor with no effect, blocking endogenous mediators.
B · Ion channels
Blockers stop permeation through the pore; modulators increase or decrease the channel's opening probability.
C · Enzymes
Inhibitors block the normal reaction; a false substrate is processed into an abnormal metabolite (and some drugs are inactive prodrugs activated by an enzyme).
D · Transporters (carriers)
Inhibitors block transport; a false substrate is carried and accumulates as an abnormal compound.
Legend
Agonist/substrate, antagonist/inhibitor, abnormal product, prodrug — the colour code used across all four panels.
Reasoning · why "know the target" is the whole game

A drug has no effect in isolation — its action is entirely a property of the target it binds and what that binding does. That's why PD is organised by target type rather than by drug: name the target and its response mode, and you can predict the drug's effect and its side-effects. It also warns of a subtlety — drugs bind acceptors too (sites like plasma proteins that bind the drug without producing a direct response), which affect its distribution but not its action.

Clinical / real-world · one target class per drug class

These four boxes organise a huge fraction of the pharmacopoeia. Receptor drugs: β-blockers, opioids, antihistamines. Ion-channel drugs: local anaesthetics (Na⁺), calcium-channel blockers, benzodiazepines (Cl⁻, §3). Enzyme drugs: ACE inhibitors, statins, aspirin (COX). Transporter drugs: SSRIs (serotonin transporter), proton-pump inhibitors, loop diuretics. Learn the target and the whole class falls into place.

Memory hook · the four targets

"RITE" targets — Receptors, Ion channels, Transporters, Enzymes. Everything a drug grabs is one of these.

R Recall checklist — drug targets
  • PK vs PD — PK: body → drug; PD: drug → body (mechanism of action).
  • Targets are mostly proteins; drugs activate, block, or modulate them.
  • Four targets (RITE) — receptors, ion channels, transporters, enzymes.
  • Modes — receptor agonist/antagonist; channel blocker/modulator; enzyme inhibitor/false substrate; transporter inhibitor.
§1Binding · L7

Specificity, selectivity & affinity

Three words for how tightly, and how choosily, a drug binds.

Before a drug can do anything it must bind — and three properties describe that binding: how exclusively it hits one target (specificity), how it prefers certain targets/tissues (selectivity), and how tightly it holds on (affinity).

Specificity & selectivity

The ideal drug would interact with only one molecular target, at one site, and have only one effect — specificity. Specificity is reciprocal (it describes both the drug for its target and the target for its drug), and no drug is completely specific. What most drugs actually show is selectivity: a preference for a molecular target in particular cells and tissues. A non-selective drug acts on more than one target at therapeutic concentration — the classic example being propranolol, a non-selective beta-blocker (it blocks β₁ and β₂).

Affinity

Affinity is the tendency of a drug to bind to the receptor — the strength of the reversible drug–receptor interaction, determined by the drug's chemical structure. It is measured by the dissociation constant KD: the concentration of drug that occupies half the receptors. The rule to burn in: a lower KD means a higher affinity (less drug needed to fill half the receptors). Plate 1.1 shows two drugs — Drug 2 reaches 50% occupancy at a lower concentration than Drug 1, so Drug 2 has the higher affinity (smaller KD).

Label Key — reading the binding curve
y-axis
Percent of receptors occupied — a binding curve, not yet a response curve.
KD
The concentration at 50% occupancy — the numerical measure of affinity. Lower KD = higher affinity.
Drug 2 (solid)
Reaches 50% at a lower concentration → higher affinity (smaller KD).
Drug 1 (dashed)
Needs more drug for 50% → lower affinity (larger KD).
Reasoning · why affinity ≠ effect

Affinity only says how well a drug sticks, not what happens once it's stuck. An antagonist can have superb affinity yet produce no response at all. That gap — between occupying a receptor and activating it — is exactly what §2 is about: occupation is governed by affinity, activation by efficacy. Holding those two ideas apart is the single most important move in pharmacodynamics.

Clinical / real-world · why selectivity is safety

Selectivity is the difference between a therapeutic effect and a side-effect. Propranolol's lack of β-selectivity means it also blocks β₂ receptors in the airways — potentially triggering bronchospasm in an asthmatic. Newer β₁-selective ("cardioselective") blockers were designed precisely to spare the lungs. No drug is perfectly specific, so most of clinical pharmacology is managing the effects a drug has beyond its intended target.

Memory hook · KD direction

Low KD = high affinity. Think "it takes only a little to fill half the seats, because the drug clings tight."

R Recall checklist — specificity, selectivity & affinity
  • Specificity — one target/site/effect (ideal, reciprocal, never complete).
  • Selectivity — preference for a target in certain cells/tissues; propranolol = non-selective β-blocker.
  • Affinity — tendency/strength of reversible binding, set by chemical structure.
  • KD — concentration at 50% occupancy; lower KD = higher affinity.
  • Occupation ≠ activation — affinity is binding, not effect.
§2Agonists · L8

Agonists, efficacy & potency

From binding to response — and how we put numbers on it.

Binding is only half the story. An agonist both occupies and activates its receptor; an antagonist occupies without activating. Plate 2.1 makes the split explicit — and it is the key to everything that follows.

Label Key — two steps, two properties
Occupation (R → AR)
The drug binds the receptor — governed by affinity. Both agonists and antagonists do this.
Activation (AR → AR*)
The occupied receptor flips to its active form — governed by efficacy. Only an agonist achieves it.
Drug A (agonist)
Occupies and activates → AR* → RESPONSE.
Drug B (antagonist)
Occupies but cannot activate (zero efficacy) → BR → NO RESPONSE.

So two properties describe an agonist: efficacy — the capacity to activate a receptor and generate a response — and potency, which is a mixed function of both affinity and efficacy. For most drugs, binding and activation are reversible, dynamic processes.

§2.1Reading the concentration–response curve

We quantify effect with a concentration–response curve (CRC): response (% of maximum) against log drug concentration. Two numbers matter:

  • Emax — the maximal response a drug can produce (the curve's height) → a measure of efficacy.
  • EC50 — the concentration producing 50% of the maximal response (the curve's horizontal position) → a measure of potency. The lower the potency, the higher the dose needed.
Label Key — three behaviours on one graph
Full agonist
Climbs to the tissue's Emax (100%) — full efficacy.
Partial agonist
Plateaus below Emax even at full occupancy — lower efficacy.
Antagonist
Flat line — affinity but zero efficacy, no response of its own.
Emax
The ceiling of response — the vertical measure of efficacy.

Plate 2.3 puts real opioids on the same axes: enkephalin, morphine and buprenorphine. Their curves sit at different positions (different potency) and reach different heights (different efficacy).

Label Key — potency & efficacy in real drugs
Enkephalin
Leftmost curve (lowest EC50) → most potent; reaches ~100% → full efficacy.
Morphine
Curve further right → less potent than enkephalin; still near-full efficacy.
Buprenorphine
Furthest right and plateaus low (~55%) → a partial agonist (lower efficacy).
Reasoning · potency and efficacy are different axes

This is the exam's favourite trap. Efficacy is vertical (how high the curve goes, Emax); potency is horizontal (how little drug it takes, EC50). A drug can be very potent but low-efficacy (buprenorphine binds tightly yet caps out at ~55%), or less potent but full-efficacy. "More potent" only means the curve sits further left — it says nothing about the maximum achievable effect. Never let "potent" and "effective" blur together.

§2.2Inverse agonists & constitutive activity

Some receptors are active without any ligand — constitutive activity, an equilibrium between inactive (Ri) and active (Ra) conformations. Against that baseline, drugs span a full spectrum of efficacy (Plate 2.4): a full agonist drives the equilibrium toward Ra; a partial agonist less so; a competitive antagonist sits at baseline; and an inverse agonist has negative efficacy — it stabilises the inactive Ri and pushes the response below resting.

Label Key — a continuum of efficacy
Baseline (100)
The constitutive activity present with no drug (Ri ⇌ Ra equilibrium).
Full / partial agonist
Positive efficacy — shift the equilibrium toward active Ra, raising response (fully / partly).
Competitive antagonist
Zero efficacy — no change from baseline when no agonist is present.
Inverse agonist
Negative efficacy — stabilises inactive Ri, pushing response below baseline.
Worked example · reading potency & efficacy off the opioid CRC (Plate 2.3)

Rank enkephalin, morphine and buprenorphine by potency and by efficacy, using only the curves.

  1. Potency = horizontal position (EC50). Read the concentration at 50% of each curve's own maximum. Enkephalin's curve is furthest left (lowest EC50), then morphine, then buprenorphine furthest right. So potency: enkephalin > morphine > buprenorphine.
  2. Efficacy = plateau height (Emax). Enkephalin and morphine both approach ~100% (full agonists); buprenorphine plateaus at ~55%. So efficacy: enkephalin ≈ morphine > buprenorphine.
  3. Classify. Enkephalin and morphine are full agonists; buprenorphine, capping well below maximum, is a partial agonist.

Answer: potency enkephalin > morphine > buprenorphine; efficacy enkephalin ≈ morphine > buprenorphine (partial). Horizontal = potency, vertical = efficacy.

Clinical / real-world · buprenorphine & inverse agonists

Buprenorphine's partial agonism is a feature, not a flaw: its ceiling on Emax means less respiratory depression at high doses, which is why it's used in opioid-dependence treatment — enough effect to prevent withdrawal, a built-in safety limit. Inverse agonists matter too: several "antihistamines" and β-blockers are technically inverse agonists, turning down receptors that idle in the "on" position even without their natural ligand.

Memory hook · potency vs efficacy

EC50 = left–right = potency (how much drug). Emax = up–down = efficacy (how big the effect). Left = strong; tall = effective.

R Recall checklist — agonists, efficacy & potency
  • Occupation (affinity) vs activation (efficacy) — AR → AR* → response.
  • Efficacy = capacity to activate (Emax, curve height); potency = affinity + efficacy (EC50, curve position).
  • Full agonist reaches Emax; partial plateaus lower; antagonist flat (zero efficacy).
  • Inverse agonist = negative efficacy — stabilises inactive receptor below constitutive baseline.
§3Antagonists · L8

Antagonists & allosteric modulation

Blocking a receptor — reversibly, permanently, or from the side.

Antagonists have affinity but zero efficacy — they block. How they block shapes the curve, and tells you whether more agonist can win the receptor back.

Competitive antagonist — surmountable

A competitive antagonist reversibly binds the same site as the agonist. Its signature (Plate 3.1): it shifts the agonist curve to the right without changing the slope or maximum (Emax). Because the block is reversible and at the same site, enough extra agonist can outcompete it — the effect is surmountable. (A partial agonist mixed with a full agonist also shifts the curve right — look at the initial response to tell them apart.) These make excellent drugs for turning down endogenous mediators.

Label Key — reading the shift
Curves 0 → 10 → 100
Increasing antagonist concentration — each shifts the agonist curve rightward.
Same Emax
Every curve still reaches 100% — the maximum is unchanged (surmountable).
Parallel shift
Slope preserved — the hallmark of competitive antagonism; more agonist overcomes it.

Irreversible antagonist — insurmountable

An irreversible antagonist forms covalent bonds with the receptor and dissociates very slowly or not at all. Its signature (Plate 3.2): it shifts the curve right and reduces the slope and maximal response (Emax) — because those receptors are permanently out of action, no amount of agonist restores the full effect (insurmountable). Few are used clinically; aspirin (irreversibly acetylating COX) is the classic example.

Label Key — the insurmountable block
Progressive right-shift
As with competitive block, higher antagonist moves the curve right…
Falling Emax
…but here the plateau also drops — receptors are permanently removed, so the ceiling falls.
Insurmountable
Extra agonist cannot restore the maximum — the defining contrast with competitive antagonism.
Reasoning · surmountable vs insurmountable, and receptor reserve

The whole distinction is can more agonist win? Competitive block is a tug-of-war at one site — reversible, so flooding the system with agonist restores full response (Emax unchanged, curve just shifted right). Irreversible block removes receptors from the game — no contest is possible, so the maximum itself falls. This also explains receptor reserve ("spare receptors"): if a tissue can hit full response without occupying every receptor, then early irreversible block only shifts the curve (spare receptors absorb the loss) before Emax finally drops — and it's why a CRC can't be used to read affinity when spare receptors exist.

Allosteric modulation

Not every drug competes at the agonist's site. An allosteric modulator binds a different site (the allosteric site, as opposed to the agonist's orthosteric site) and increases (positive) or decreases (negative) the agonist's effect — like a dimmer switch on the main light. The exemplar (Plate 3.3): benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators of the GABAA receptor — they don't open the channel themselves, but make GABA better at doing so.

Label Key — orthosteric vs allosteric
Orthosteric site
Where the natural agonist GABA binds to open the channel.
Allosteric site
A separate site where a modulator (e.g. a benzodiazepine) binds — it doesn't open the channel alone.
Cl⁻ flux
When GABA binds, the channel opens and chloride flows in, inhibiting the neuron.
Positive modulator
Enhances GABA's effect (more channel opening) — the basis of benzodiazepine sedation.
Clinical / real-world · the antagonists & modulators you'll meet

These mechanisms name real drugs. Competitive antagonists: naloxone reversing an opioid overdose (out-competed at the μ-receptor), most β-blockers, antihistamines. Irreversible: aspirin, whose covalent COX block lasts the platelet's lifetime — the reason low-dose aspirin thins blood for days. Positive allosteric modulators: benzodiazepines for anxiety and seizures, boosting GABA rather than flooding the brain with a raw agonist — which is part of why they're safer in overdose than older sedatives.

Memory hook · which block, which curve

Competitive = "outcompeted": right shift, same Emax (surmountable). Irreversible = "immovable": right shift + lower Emax (insurmountable). Orthosteric = the original site; allosteric = another site.

R Recall checklist — antagonists & modulation
  • Competitive antagonist — same site, reversible; right-shift, Emax unchanged (surmountable).
  • Irreversible antagonist — covalent (e.g. aspirin); right-shift + reduced Emax (insurmountable).
  • Receptor reserve — spare receptors; CRC can't give affinity when they exist.
  • Allosteric modulator — binds a non-orthosteric site; positive/negative (benzodiazepines = positive on GABAA).
